about.title: About me
about.p1: I joined École 42 without knowing what to expect, and I discovered software development through hands-on practice, from low-level C programming to complete web applications. After exploring both front-end and back-end development, I found my place in full-stack work. What I love is building tools that are truly useful to the people who use them, and finally seeing everything work after a long debugging session.
about.p2: I've completed the core curriculum and I'm now working towards 42's RNCP Level 7 qualification. I'm looking for a work-study position (or an internship) starting in November 2026, to join a team where I can contribute and keep learning new technologies.
about.p3: Before 42, I spent two years in a work-study program, so I know how to balance work and studies.

ft_transcendence.overview: A collaborative project management web app, Trello-style. Users create an organization and several projects, then assign and track tasks on a board.
ft_transcendence.role: Team lead: organizing and distributing the work. I built the front-end and connected it to the back-end through API calls.
ft_transcendence.challenge: At one point, every fix caused new regressions. We sorted bugs by impact to fix first the ones breaking other features, gave each part a clear owner, and synced the code after every change so everyone always worked on an up-to-date base.

ft_irc.overview: A messaging server that handles multiple connected clients at the same time, with private messages and channels. Like Discord, without a graphical interface.
ft_irc.role: Team lead. I set up concurrent connection handling with poll(), implemented most of the IRC commands and some of the protocol's error replies, and built the bonus: a bot that automatically joins a channel and replies to users.
ft_irc.tests: Tested with irssi, a real IRC client, and with netcat, so the server follows the protocol used by existing clients.

minishell.overview: A simplified Unix shell inspired by bash, written in C. It reads and parses commands, then executes them with support for pipes, redirections, heredoc, environment variables and signals.
minishell.role: I built the builtins (cd, echo, export…) and most of the execution: process creation with fork and execve, pipes, redirections and signal handling.
minishell.challenge: Making the parsing and the execution, each developed separately, work together. Combining them revealed many bugs, especially with heredoc, which has to read user input, handle signals and pass its content to the right command.

cub3d.overview: A first-person game engine, Wolfenstein 3D-style, written in C. From a 2D map, it renders a textured 3D maze that the player can move through in real time.
cub3d.role: I built the entire raycasting: casting one ray per screen column, computing the distance to the wall it hits, then deriving the height of the wall to draw to create the illusion of 3D.
cub3d.challenge: The geometry, especially the fish-eye effect, which curved the walls at the edges of the screen. It's fixed by using the perpendicular distance to the camera plane instead of the actual length of the ray.

inception.overview: A complete web infrastructure split into several services, each running in its own Docker container: an NGINX server secured with TLS, a WordPress site and a MariaDB database, orchestrated with Docker Compose. Every image is built from my own Dockerfile, without any ready-made image.
inception.learned: This was the project that challenged me the most: meticulous configuration, dense documentation, containers that refused to talk to each other, and errors that were hard to diagnose from inside a container. But it's also the one that taught me to read logs to understand why a container crashes, to write and read a docker-compose.yml file, and to understand why a project works on one machine but not on another. I reused these skills directly to run ft_transcendence with Docker.
